 Follow Us On: News Technology News Microsoft told him to move back to India after H-1B denial. He built Snapdeal Microsoft told him to move back to India after H-1B denial. He built Snapdeal
 An Indian employee's H-1B petition was rejected while he was working at Microsoft in the US. The company suggested he move to India and reapply after a year, but he chose to start his own business. Interestingly, companies like IBM have stopped sponsoring visas for most roles in their US consulting division.
 Advertisement H-1B visa rejection led Kunal Bahl from Microsoft to founding Snapdeal. (Image credit: Reuters) By: Ankita Garg New Delhi , Nov 16, 2026 23:24 IST Last Updated Nov 16, 2026 23:24 IST Published by Ankita Garg Nov 16, 2026 19:28 IST A job at Microsoft did not guarantee an Indian employee a work visa in the US. In 2007, Kunal Bahl, who was then working at the technology giant, found his H-1B petition rejected. Microsoft suggested that he relocate to India and continue working from there while making another attempt at securing the visa a year later.
 Bahl, who later co-founded Snapdeal and investment firm Titan Capital, has recalled the experience in an interview with Business Insider. He said the rejection came in June or July 2007, when he was waiting for the outcome of his visa application and approaching the end of his temporary work authorisation in the US.
 advertisement ❮ ❯ Read Full Story He had graduated from the University of Pennsylvania and joined Microsoft as a full-time employee in October 2006, following an internship at the company. The visa decision caught him off guard. He said he initially struggled to understand why his application had been rejected despite being employed by a major technology company.
 After speaking to Microsoft's team, he understood that the decision was final. The company offered him an option to work from its India office and try for the H-1B again after 12 months. But Bahl did not want to return to India simply to continue his corporate career. He decided to use the move as an opportunity to pursue an idea he had considered for years - starting a business.
 He contacted his school friend Rohit Bansal, and the two set up a company in September 2007, shortly before Bahl arrived in India. They began with a coupon-book business, which eventually developed into e-commerce platform Snapdeal.
 IBM stops H-1B and green card sponsorship for most consulting jobs
 Meanwhile, IBM has decided to discontinue H-1B visa and green card sponsorship for most positions in its consulting business in the US. The move gives affected employees a choice between continuing their jobs from outside the country and leaving the company by the end of 2026, according to Bloomberg.
 The company said the decision was linked to changing hiring requirements and the availability of skilled professionals. An IBM spokesperson told Newsweek that the company's participation in high-skilled immigration programs had been declining for several years.
 IBM said it had previously used these programs to fill skill shortages but would no longer sponsor visas and green cards for the majority of roles within IBM Consulting.
 The decision comes amid increased scrutiny of employment-based immigration in the US under the Donald Trump administration. Microsoft and Adobe were among companies whose access to the green card labour certification process was suspended in October over alleged violations.
 The Permanent Labour Certification program, commonly known as PERM, is an important step for employers seeking green cards for foreign workers. Companies must generally demonstrate that there are no qualified and available US workers for the position before sponsoring an employee for permanent residency. - Ends
